title: Six Thousand Seafarers Are Trapped in the Gulf. For Indian Sailors, the War Has Become Personal.
excerpt: Three Indian crew members are dead. One sailor watched 140 missiles fly in 30 minutes. Thousands more are stranded on ships running low on food and fuel. India is sending diplomats. The sailors want a way home.
body:
India is among the world's top three suppliers of merchant seafarers, with a workforce roughly 300,000 strong. Thousands of them are now caught in the crossfire of a war they have no part in — stranded on rusting ships in the Persian Gulf, watching missiles streak across the sky at night, and wondering whether their own government can bring them home.

One Indian sailor, speaking to reporters after returning from two and a half months trapped on a vessel in the Gulf, described seeing approximately 140 missiles fired within a single thirty-minute window. "We are pawns," he said. "The world talks about us only when they see a dead body. I don't know why everyone is waiting for a dead body before the entire nation talks about sailors."

## A Crisis of Staggering Scale

The numbers paint a bleak picture. According to the International Maritime Organization, roughly 6,000 seafarers remain stranded on hundreds of ships in the Persian Gulf, unable to safely leave. German insurer Allianz estimates that around 1,150 cargo-carrying vessels — with a combined vessel and cargo value of approximately $125 billion — are effectively trapped.

Three Indian crew members have been killed since the conflict began in February, and another remains missing. The most devastating incident came when a U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions into the engine room of the Palau-flagged tanker Settebello, which carried 24 Indian mariners. India took the rare step of lodging a second formal protest with Washington, with the foreign ministry summoning the American chargé d'affaires to convey "its deep concern over the use of lethal and deadly force against civilian shipping."

## Life Under Fire

The accounts from returning sailors are harrowing. Tithi Chiranjeevi, a 28-year-old from Visakhapatnam, described being stranded for more than a month outside Iran's port of Khorramshahr. "Around 10 to 20 missiles struck every night. No one could sleep," he told Reuters after finally making it home via a gruelling 15-day journey through Iraq, Armenia, and Dubai.

As food ran out and satellite communication links snapped — Starlink was cut — Chiranjeevi lost contact with his widowed mother for weeks. His colleague, Anant Singh Chauhan from Uttar Pradesh, put it more plainly: "Sometimes, we used to feel we won't be able to make it back home."

Both men had borrowed 450,000 rupees each — roughly $4,800 — at exorbitant interest rates from relatives and moneylenders to secure their shipping jobs. Returning home without pay, traumatised, and in debt is their reward.

## The Hormuz Chokepoint

The Strait of Hormuz, a 104-mile waterway, carried one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas before the war. Iran has since largely taken control of the passage, establishing what it calls the Persian Gulf Strait Authority to collect tolls and regulate traffic. The U.N. shipping agency's governing council on Friday "strongly condemned" this unilateral power grab, calling on all 176 member states to reject Iran's sovereignty claim.

But condemnation has not reopened the strait. This week, after Iranian forces struck three commercial tankers — including Qatari and Saudi vessels — the Joint Maritime Information Center raised the threat level to "severe," the second-highest on its five-tier scale. War-risk insurance premiums have surged to eight times normal rates, covering only 2 to 4 per cent of hull value. Eight of the world's largest container carriers have suspended Hormuz transits entirely.

Daily traffic through the strait, which averaged 125 to 140 ships before the conflict, had barely recovered to about 40 per day before this week's escalation knocked it back again.

## India's Diplomatic Tightrope

India has been walking a careful line. Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar spoke directly with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araqchi to press the case for shipping safety and the safe return of Indian crew. Separately, India opened direct talks with Tehran to secure passage for nine trapped Indian-flagged tankers and 198 stranded sailors.

The Indian government says it has helped bring roughly 3,000 sailors safely home from the Gulf region since the conflict began. But maritime unions and opposition politicians say that is not nearly enough. The government has been criticised for relying on diplomatic protests rather than organising large-scale evacuations of the kind it has mounted for Indian nationals trapped in other conflict zones.

## What Comes Next

Iran's foreign minister arrived in Oman on Saturday for fresh talks on the strait, with Washington seeking a public pledge of free and secure transit. U.S. Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and special envoy Steve Witkoff were reportedly expected to lead negotiations. But Iran's state media said no talks would take place until the U.S. "retreated from its positions."

For the thousands of Indian seafarers still stuck in the Gulf — some on ships running low on fuel, food, and drinking water — the diplomacy is cold comfort. As one sailor put it: "The company I work for has released us from duty and we are now waiting for safe passage because flights from Tehran are not operating. If we get clearance to sail to the Middle East or anywhere nearby, we will dock there and take the earliest flight home."

Until that clearance comes, they wait.
